sections.heading: You made the first move toward peace
sections.text:
Lord God Almighty, you did not wait for me to find my way back to you. I was the one in the wrong, yet you moved toward sinners first. Through the cross of Jesus, you opened the way for peace, and now you call me to receive the reconciliation you have already provided.

So help me not to doubt your willingness to save. If you, the offended God, have come near with mercy, then the real problem is not any reluctance in you. It is the stubborn foolishness in me that resists grace.
theological_themes: God initiates reconciliation with sinners through Christ’s cross; the gospel is not God being persuaded by us, but God calling us to receive the peace he has made.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that reconciliation begins with God, who acts in Christ and then sends the appeal to be reconciled to him. This directly grounds the prayer’s emphasis that God makes the first move and calls sinners to receive peace.

This passage speaks of people being reconciled to God through the death of his Son while they were enemies. It supports the prayer’s focus on the cross as the place where God’s saving initiative meets human hostility.

sections.heading: Do not let me pretend my resistance is harmless
sections.text:
Father, if I refuse to come to you for mercy, I am not being independent or thoughtful or strong. I am living as if I do not need you. I am treating your kindness with contempt. I am holding on to anger, pride, and self-rule, and you name that for what it is: enmity against you.

Please show me the truth about my heart without letting me hide from it. Let me see how unreasonable it is to stand away from you when you are offering me peace.
theological_themes: Human refusal of God’s grace is moral hostility, not neutral independence; self-sufficiency and pride are part of sin’s rebellion against God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes sinners as alienated and hostile in mind, yet reconciled through Christ’s death. This supports the prayer’s confession that resistance to God is real enmity, and that reconciliation comes only through Christ.
This passage names the mindset of the flesh as hostile to God and unable to submit to him. It gives biblical weight to the prayer’s refusal to treat self-rule as harmless.

sections.heading: Teach me to cling to Christ, not to myself
sections.text:
You have shown me that I need a Mediator. I need your Messiah, Jesus, and I need him with my whole heart.

I need him as King, because I cannot safely rule myself. I need him as Prophet, because I cannot guide myself into truth. I need him as Priest, because I cannot take away my own sin or defeat death by my own strength.

So teach me to stop trusting my own wisdom, my own obedience, and my own power to conquer sin. Teach me to hold fast to your beloved Son, who is able to do for me what I could never do for myself.
theological_themes: Christ is the necessary Mediator who rules, reveals God, and deals with sin; faith means turning from self-reliance and depending wholly on him.

scripture_references.connection: Paul identifies Jesus Christ as the one Mediator between God and humanity who gave himself as a ransom. This grounds the prayer’s insistence that access to God and rescue from sin come through Christ, not through self-effort.

Hebrews presents the Son as God’s final word, the one who made purification for sins, and the one seated in royal authority. This illuminates the prayer’s language of Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King.

sections.heading: Keep me trusting and repenting every day
sections.text:
Lord, saving me is Christ’s work. I cannot add to it or complete it. But you call me to keep trusting him, to keep holding on to him by faith.

And with that faith, keep giving me daily repentance. Let me grieve the sin that Jesus has already carried away by grace. Do not let forgiveness make me careless. Let it make me honest, humble, and quick to return to you.
theological_themes: Salvation is accomplished by Christ and received by faith; ongoing repentance is the believer’s daily response to grace, not a payment for forgiveness.

scripture_references.connection: This passage teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not human achievement, while also showing that grace produces a changed life. It supports the distinction between Christ’s saving work and the believer’s faith-filled response.
John writes to believers about honest confession and God’s faithful forgiveness. This supports the prayer’s request for ongoing repentance without implying that repentance earns salvation.

sections.heading: Let the cross be my peace
sections.text:
Keep teaching me that faith receives the righteousness of Christ. His righteousness satisfies your justice, and it also shows me how deeply you love me. The cross is not only the answer to my guilt; it is the proof that your heart is for me in Christ.

Help me build my peace on what Jesus has done, not on how steady I feel or how well I think I am doing. Let his finished work be the ground of my confidence that you accept me, a sinner, by grace.

Keep me near the cross, Father. Let me live there with a clear conscience, a softened heart, and a steady trust in your mercy.
theological_themes: Christ’s righteousness is the believer’s ground of peace with God; the cross satisfies justice, displays divine love, and assures sinners of acceptance by grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul explains that God justifies sinners through faith in Christ, showing both his righteousness and his mercy. This supports the prayer’s concern that the cross satisfies justice while becoming the ground of peace.
This passage connects justification by faith with peace with God and access into grace. It directly supports the prayer’s desire to rest acceptance on Christ’s work rather than personal performance.

John presents the sending of the Son as the revelation of God’s love, especially in his atoning work. This supports the prayer’s claim that Christ’s righteousness and sacrifice are evidence of God’s love for the sinner.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The taxonomy supplied does not include an approved tag id for reconciliation, though reconciliation is the central theme of the prayer. Because tags must use only supplied ids, this theme should be handled as a suggested tag rather than an approved tag if strict validation is required.

The original phrase that God has “reconciled thyself to the world” is theologically delicate, since Scripture more commonly says God reconciles sinners or the world to himself in Christ. The adaptation renders this as God opening the way for peace and calling sinners to receive reconciliation, in line with 2 Corinthians 5:18-21.

The original’s statement that “to cleave to him by faith is my work” could be misunderstood as making faith a meritorious contribution to salvation. The adaptation preserves the responsibility to trust Christ while clarifying that salvation itself is Christ’s work and grace, not human achievement.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Thy overtures of grace” was rendered as God moving toward sinners first and calling the sinner to receive reconciliation, preserving the original’s emphasis on divine initiative without reproducing archaic diplomatic language.
The threefold description of Christ as king, prophet, and priest was retained explicitly because it is central to the original’s account of why a Mediator is necessary.

“Live always near the cross” was rendered as building peace on Christ’s finished work and living with a clear conscience, softened heart, and steady trust, to express the practical spiritual posture intended by the original.
